p: If I were asked to name the single change that has most altered the condition of mankind, I should not name the steam engine, nor the printing press, nor the discovery of America. I should name the sowing of seed. For some three hundred thousand years our kind lived by hunting animals and gathering wild plants, moving with the seasons, owning little more than could be carried. Then, beginning about twelve thousand years ago, in several regions of the world independently, people began to plant and harvest crops and to keep animals in herds. Within a few thousand years the greater part of mankind had become farmers, and the world was changed beyond recognition.

The learned of the twentieth century called this the Neolithic Revolution, the word Neolithic meaning simply the New Stone Age, because the first farmers still used tools of stone, though finely ground and polished. The phrase was coined by an Australian archaeologist named Vere Gordon Childe in the nineteen twenties. It is a good phrase, so long as we remember that this revolution took several thousand years, and that nobody who lived through it knew that it was happening.

The earliest farming of which we have good evidence arose in the region the scholars call the Fertile Crescent: a great arc of land curving from the valley of the Nile, up through Palestine and Syria, across the south of Turkey, and down through the valleys of the Tigris and Euphrates to the Persian Gulf. Here, from about eleven or twelve thousand years ago, people began to cultivate wheat of the kinds called emmer and einkorn, and barley, lentils, peas, chickpeas and flax. They began to keep sheep and goats, and later cattle and pigs.

It is important to understand that farming was invented more than once. In China, millet was cultivated in the north and rice in the valley of the Yangtze from about nine thousand years ago. In the highlands of New Guinea, people grew taro and bananas. In Mexico, maize was bred over thousands of years from a wild grass called teosinte, whose ear is so small and hard that one would never suppose it the ancestor of the corn cob; there too were domesticated beans and squashes. In the Andes of South America, potatoes and the llama. In Africa, sorghum and certain kinds of rice and yams. Each region found its own plants and its own animals, and the Encyclopaedia counts something like a dozen independent beginnings.

How it happened is a matter of patient argument. No one sat down and invented agriculture. The process seems to have been gradual. People who harvested wild grain year after year, cutting it with sickles of flint and storing it, unconsciously favoured those plants whose seeds stayed on the stalk instead of scattering to the ground, for those were the ones they gathered and, when they spilled some near their dwellings, sowed. Over generations the plants changed, until they could no longer seed themselves without human help. Wheat, in a sense, domesticated us as much as we domesticated it. We became its servants: clearing ground for it, protecting it, carrying it to new lands.

One of the most surprising discoveries reported in the Encyclopaedia concerns a hill in southern Turkey called Göbekli Tepe, which in Turkish means, I am told, the hill with a navel, or potbelly hill. Here, from about eleven and a half thousand years ago, people raised great circles of stone pillars, some of them more than five metres high, carved with foxes, boars, snakes, scorpions and vultures, and with arms and hands that show the pillars to be stylised persons. The men who built them did so before there was any settled farming nearby, or at the very beginning of it. The German archaeologist who excavated the place, Klaus Schmidt, called it a temple, and argued that the need to feed the crowds who gathered to build and worship there may have been one of the reasons people began to farm. "First came the temple, then the city," he is quoted as saying. Later scholars have found houses and signs of daily life at the site, and doubt that it was only a temple. But it remains astonishing that monuments so elaborate were raised by people who had not yet settled into villages.

Farming allowed people to stay in one place, and staying in one place allowed people to accumulate. Villages grew into towns. The most remarkable of the early towns is Çatalhöyük, also in Turkey, inhabited from about nine thousand years ago, where several thousand people lived in houses of mud brick packed so tightly together that there were no streets; they walked across the roofs and entered their houses by ladders through holes in the ceiling. They buried their dead beneath the floors of their houses, painted their walls with scenes of hunting and of vultures, and set the horns of wild bulls into their walls and benches. The houses are strikingly similar in size, and the excavators have found little evidence of chiefs or palaces. It may have been, for a time, a society of something like equals. It did not last.

I have called farming the greatest change in human history, and I do not retract it. But it was not an unmixed blessing, and the men of the future are much more candid about this than my own contemporaries. The skeletons of early farmers are, on average, shorter than those of the hunters before them, with worse teeth and more signs of disease and malnutrition. A diet founded upon a few grains is poorer than one gathered from a hundred wild sources. Animals kept close by brought their diseases into the human household; many of our worst plagues, measles and smallpox and influenza among them, came to us from our herds. Crowded settlements bred infection. A failed harvest, which a wandering band could escape by moving on, meant famine for a village tied to its fields.

And farming made possible, for the first time, great inequalities. A hunter cannot accumulate much, for he must carry it; a farmer can fill a granary, and a granary can be guarded, inherited, taxed and seized. Land became property; property required defence; defence required warriors; warriors required feeding; and before very long there were kings, and slaves, and armies, and the whole melancholy and magnificent apparatus of civilisation. One learned man of the future, Professor Jared Diamond, went so far as to call farming the worst mistake in the history of the human race. That is an exaggeration, as provocative titles generally are. Without farming there could be no cities, no writing, no libraries, and no learned professors to call it a mistake. But it is wholesome to be reminded that every great advance is purchased, and that the purchasers are not always those who enjoy the goods.
